summary: Describes a Telnet option that lets a client tell a Telnet server how large its window is. It was a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you log in remotely, the far computer doesn't know how big your screen is. This option lets your computer tell it.

questions: what is telnet window size option
how does telnet send terminal size
subtitle: How a Telnet client tells the server how many columns and rows its window has.

tldr.problem: A Telnet client often runs in a window whose size can change, and the server needs the size for proper cursor control.
tldr.mechanism: The NAWS option (code 31) is negotiated with the usual WILL/DO mechanism, and the client then sends a subnegotiation with the width and height in characters, as two 16-bit values.
tldr.outcome: The client can resend the size whenever the window changes. The information is advisory, so a server may ignore it.

facts.label: Value size
facts.value: 2 bytes each for width and height

today: RFC 1073 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Report the Window Size
sections.content:
With windowing systems, a Telnet client is often run inside a variable-sized window. The server needs to know the window size for proper cursor control, and the size may change during the session. NAWS (Negotiate About Window Size) lets the client send the height and width in characters to the server.

The RFC says the older options for output line width (NAOL) and page size (NAOP) do not have the right semantics. They are bidirectional, so the server might control the client's size, and they are limited to 253 characters per axis. NAWS lets the client keep total control of its window and raises the limit to 65535.
sections.plainLanguage: Your window can change size, and the computer on the other end needs to know so it draws things in the right place. This option is how the client tells it.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The option name is NAWS and its code is 31. The client sends IAC WILL NAWS or the server sends IAC DO NAWS to suggest using it, and either side can refuse with WON'T or DON'T. The default is WON'T NAWS and DON'T NAWS, so no window size is assumed.

If both sides agree, the client may send a subnegotiation, and may send it again if the user changes the window size. Some server operating systems cannot take updates, so the server may send DON'T NAWS to forbid further subnegotiation. The RFC notes that a negotiation loop will not form under these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two computers ask each other if they want to talk about window size. If both say yes, the client can send the size, and again whenever it changes.

sections.title: The Size Subnegotiation
sections.content:
The subnegotiation is IAC SB NAWS WIDTH[1] WIDTH[0] HEIGHT[1] HEIGHT[0] IAC SE. Width and height are each two bytes in the Internet standard byte and bit order, so the maximum is 65535 characters. Any 255 in the data must be doubled to tell it apart from the IAC character.

A value of zero means that no width (or height) is being sent. The server then assumes a value that is operating system specific, probably based on the terminal type if one was sent with the TERMINAL TYPE option. The information is advisory, and a server may accept the option but not use the size.
sections.plainLanguage: The size is sent as two numbers, width then height. A zero means the client is not saying, so the server makes its own guess.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
In the RFC's first example, the server sends IAC DO NAWS and the client answers IAC WILL NAWS. The client then sends IAC SB NAWS 0 80 0 24 IAC SE, a window 80 characters wide and 24 high. Later it sends IAC SB NAWS 0 80 0 64 IAC SE after the user changes the height to 64.

The RFC also shows the client suggesting and the server agreeing (a width of 300 sent as 1 44), and refusals from either side. For implementers, it suggests a BSD client could catch the SIGWINCH signal and send a new subnegotiation, and the server could pass a SIGWINCH on to its child, probably a shell.
sections.plainLanguage: Say the window is 80 wide and 24 tall: the client sends 80 and 24. Make it taller and it sends 80 and 64.

fields.name: WIDTH[1]
fields.desc: High byte of the window width in characters.

fields.name: HEIGHT[1]
fields.desc: High byte of the window height in characters.

references.text: Reynolds, J., and J. Postel, "Official Internet Protocols", RFC 1011.
